**Launchly – Tech Stack & System Architecture**

*Frontend, backend and database technologies, and how the components interact*

# **1\. Overview**

Launchly is a recruitment platform built as a web application (responsive, works well on mobile) with three main parts:

* **Frontend:** renders the user interface.  
* **Backend:** handles business logic and exposes the API.  
* **Database:** stores the data.

In addition, the backend integrates external services: file storage (local disk in development, Amazon S3 in deployment), an AI service (Google's Gemini API), an email service (Gmail SMTP in development, Amazon SES in deployment) and sign-in with a Google account (OAuth 2.0).

# **2\. Selected tech stack**

| Component | Technology | Role and rationale |
| :---- | :---- | :---- |
| **Frontend** | Next.js  (React \+ TypeScript), Tailwind CSS | Builds the responsive web UI. Next.js supports server-side rendering, so job listing pages load quickly and are search-engine friendly. |
| **Backend** | Express.js  (Node.js \+ TypeScript), REST API | Handles business logic, authentication and authorization, data access and calls to external services, exposed through a REST API.  Express.js is simple, needs little configuration, and is quick to learn and deploy, which suits the limited time. It uses the same language (TypeScript) as the frontend; code is organized by technical layer (route – controller – service – data access), so adding or changing features does not change the overall structure. |
| **Database** | PostgreSQL | Data with clear relationships (users, business data and the links between them). Supports text search and stores JSON data (for example results returned by the AI). |
| AI service | Gemini API (Google AI Studio) | The backend sends text content plus instructions (a prompt) to the Gemini API and receives a structured result (JSON) to store and display. Our team does not train its own models. |
| Authentication | Google OAuth 2.0; auth token (e.g. JWT) | Supports sign-in with a Google account (Google acts as the identity provider) alongside regular sign-in. After sign-in, the backend issues a token used to authenticate subsequent requests. |

The two services below differ between the development (dev) and production deployment (deploy) environments. The code accesses them through an abstraction layer (a file-storage module and an email module), so switching environments only requires a configuration change, not changes to business logic.

| Component | Dev | Deploy | Rationale |
| :---- | :---- | :---- | :---- |
| File storage | Local file storage: files saved to a folder on the machine/server, uploaded with Multer | Amazon S3 (private bucket) | Dev: free, no cloud account needed.  Deploy: files are not lost when the server restarts or is redeployed, and storage can scale and be encrypted. The database only stores the file path/key. |
| Email | Gmail SMTP via Nodemailer (App Password) | Amazon SES (via Nodemailer or SDK); alternatives: Resend/SendGrid | Dev: free and quick to set up.  Deploy: Gmail limits the number of emails per day and is more likely to be flagged as spam; SES is built for transactional email and requires verifying the sending domain. |

**Note:** *The technologies above can be changed to match the team's skills (for example, a Spring Boot or Django backend); the architecture below stays the same.*

# **3\. Architecture overview**

The system follows a three-tier client–server model (Presentation – Application – Data). The backend is organized as a modular monolith: a single application whose code is split by business function, where every function goes through the same technical layers: Routes & Controllers (receive requests), Auth & Access Control (authentication, authorization), Services (business logic) and Data Access (database access through the ORM). When feature requirements change, only the relevant module is added or modified and the overall architecture stays the same. This suits a small team with limited time and avoids the need for microservices at the early stage.

# **4\. How the components interact**

| Interaction | Description |
| :---- | :---- |
| Users ↔ Frontend | Users access the system through a web browser (HTTPS). The frontend renders the interface appropriate to the signed-in user. |
| Frontend ↔ Backend | The frontend calls the backend's REST API and data is exchanged as JSON. After sign-in, every request carries authentication information; the backend checks identity and access rights before returning a result. |
| Backend ↔ Database | The backend reads/writes PostgreSQL through an ORM (e.g. Prisma). All business data is stored here. The frontend never accesses the database directly. |
| Backend ↔ Supporting services | The backend is the only component that talks to external services: storing/reading files (local disk in dev, Amazon S3 in deploy), calling the Gemini API, and sending email (Gmail SMTP in dev, Amazon SES in deploy). API keys and other secrets live only in the backend and are never exposed to the frontend. |
| System ↔ Google (OAuth) | When signing in with Google, the user authenticates with Google; the backend verifies the result with Google and then finds or creates the matching account in the database. |

## **Flow 1: a regular request (read/write data)**

1\. The user acts in the interface; the frontend calls the REST API with authentication information.

2\. The backend checks identity and access rights.

3\. The services layer runs the business logic and reads/writes PostgreSQL through the ORM.

4\. The backend returns the result as JSON; the frontend displays it to the user.

## **Flow 2: a request that uploads a file**

1\. The frontend sends the file to the backend (multipart/form-data).

2\. The backend checks permissions, file type and size.

3\. The backend saves the file to File Storage (local in dev, S3 in deploy) and stores the file path/key in PostgreSQL.

4\. When the file is needed, the backend checks permissions before returning it to the user.
